source: Had you descended from the Pequod’s try-works to the Pequod’s forecastle, where the off duty watch were sleeping, for one single moment you would have almost thought you were standing in some illuminated shrine of canonized kings and counsellors. There they lay in their triangular oaken vaults, each mariner a chiselled muteness; a score of lamps flashing upon his hooded eyes.

In merchantmen, oil for the sailor is more scarce than the milk of queens. To dress in the dark, and eat in the dark, and stumble in darkness to his pallet, this is his usual lot. But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light. He makes his berth an Aladdin’s lamp, and lays him down in it; so that in the pitchiest night the ship’s black hull still houses an illumination.

See with what entire freedom the whaleman takes his handful of lamps—often but old bottles and vials, though—to the copper cooler at the try-works, and replenishes them there, as mugs of ale at a vat. He burns, too, the purest of oil, in its unmanufactured, and, therefore, unvitiated state; a fluid unknown to solar, lunar, or astral contrivances ashore. It is sweet as early grass butter in April. He goes and hunts for his oil, so as to be sure of its freshness and genuineness, even as the traveller on the prairie hunts up his own supper of game.

modern_en.title: Chapter 97 — The Lamp
paragraphs: If you had gone down from the Pequod's try-works to the Pequod's forecastle, where the off-duty watch lay asleep, you would almost have thought for one moment that you were standing in some lit-up shrine of sainted kings and counselors. There they lay in their three-cornered oak vaults, each sailor a carved silence, with a score of lamps flashing on his hooded eyes.

In merchant ships, oil for the sailor is more scarce than the milk of queens. To dress in the dark, eat in the dark, and stumble in darkness to his bed — this is his usual lot. But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light. He makes his bunk an Aladdin's lamp and lies down in it, so that in the blackest night the ship's dark hull still houses an illumination.

See with what perfect freedom the whaleman takes his handful of lamps — often only old bottles and vials, though — to the copper cooler at the try-works and refills them there, as mugs of ale at a vat. He burns, too, the purest of oil, in its unprocessed and therefore untainted state — a fluid unknown to solar, lunar, or astral lamps on shore. It is sweet as early grass butter in April. He goes and hunts for his oil, so as to be sure of its freshness and genuineness, even as the traveler on the prairie hunts up his own supper of game.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 97 — Lampen
paragraphs: Hvis du var gået ned fra Pequods tranværk til Pequods mandskabsrum, hvor den afgåede vagt lå og sov, ville du et øjeblik næsten have troet, at du stod i en oplyst helligdom for hellige konger og rådgivere. Der lå de i deres trekantede egehvælvinger, hver sømand en udskåret tavshed, med en snes lamper flammende over sine tilhyllede øjne.

På handelsskibe er olie til sømanden sjældnere end dronningers mælk. At klæde sig på i mørke, spise i mørke og snuble i mørke til sin køje — det er hans sædvanlige lod. Men hvalfangeren lever i lys, så sandt som han søger lysets føde. Han gør sin køje til en Aladdins lampe og lægger sig i den, så der selv i den sorteste nat er en belysning i skibets mørke skrog.

Se med hvilken fuldkommen frihed hvalfangeren tager sin håndfuld lamper — ofte dog kun gamle flasker og glas — med hen til kobberkøleren ved tranværket og fylder dem der, som man fylder ølkrus fra et kar. Han brænder også den reneste olie, i dens uforarbejdede og derfor uplettede tilstand — en væske, der er ukendt for solar-, lunar- og astrallamper på land. Den er sød som smør fra det tidlige forårsgræs i april. Han går ud og jager sin olie, for at være sikker på, at den er frisk og ægte, ligesom den rejsende på prærien jager sit eget aftensmåltid af vildt.
